title: ‘Ara-Pinarayi’ or CEO? Satheesan opens up on power, factional politics and reforms he wants for Kerala
content: Is VD Satheesan becoming an Ara-Pinarayi (half-Pinarayi Vijayan) or is Kerala getting a Chief Minister who operates more like a corporate CEO? At the Manorama News Conclave in Kochi, when Satheesan was asked about his critics' comparisons between his firm, combative style and that of former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, he embraced both labels in his own way, offering a candid account of his leadership style, his approach to coalition politics and the administrative changes he believes Kerala can no longer postpone. Responding to observations that his administrative firmness and combative posture mirror former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, Satheesan responded with a mix of humour and candour. I closely observe and take good qualities from all CMs before me. If I adopt Pinarayi's good qualities, why is 'Ara-Pinarayi' a problem? he countered with his signature 'pookie CM' smile. Pinarayi Vijayan has his own positive and negative traits; V D Satheesan has his own positive and negative traits. I retain my strengths while continuously discarding my flaws. If I adopt the good qualities of Pinarayi Vijayan as well, then being called 'Ara-Pinarayi' isn't a mistake after all, he said. But Satheesan said there was one major difference he would not compromise on — his accessibility to the media. He pointed out that Pinarayi Vijayan's press conferences often involved long prepared statements followed by a limited number of questions. In press conferences, Pinarayi Vijayan used to read out prepared text for 50 minutes and take barely five questions. If I conduct a press meet like that, you will call me 'Muzhu-Pinarayi' (full Pinarayi). Instead, I speak for 10 minutes and open the floor to all journalists until every single question is answered said Satheesan. 'Zero factionalism' Addressing the perception of operating as a lone wolf after becoming the CM without a dedicated faction within the Congress party or the UDF, Satheesan described the absence of group backing as a strategic strength that enabled the UDF's revival. In 2021, when the leadership entrusted me with the responsibility of Opposition Leader, the political atmosphere was pathetic. Congress had only 21 members in the Legislative Assembly. Had I pursued factionalism like others, 75% to 80% of my time would have been wasted on 'group management'. By not doing that, I was able to dedicate 100% of my time to reviving the UDF, he said. He also dismissed the suggestion that legislators in the ruling coalition would need to be separately appeased to keep the government together. All our MLAs stand firmly with our collective team. Why should there be any separate appeasement? There is no need for that, he said. He argued that the numbers speak for themselves. Congress's strength rose from 21 MLAs, while the UDF's tally increased from around 40 to 102. They know very well how our tally rose from 21 to 63 Congress MLAs, and from 40-odd to 102 UDF MLAs. When results are delivered, everyone shares the credit, said Satheesan. When CM thinks like a CEO When asked whether his centralized monitoring of departments resembled a corporate executive rather than a conventional politician, Satheesan did not shy away from the comparison and said there are situations in which a CM has to think like a CEO. You asked if I am a CM or a CEO. Sometimes, one may have to function like a CEO in a private enterprise to ensure results. I am ready to act decisively like a CEO when required, he said. For Satheesan, the larger problem is not executive intervention but the absence of accountability when government projects spiral out of control. Nobody is accountable in government when a 100-cr project stretches to 1,000 cr over 10 years, he said, adding that his government would formulate strict project protocols and fix liability. He cited several instances to illustrate the kind of fast decision-making he wants from the administration...
